originals.text: This layered view has an important methodological consequence. There is no single exact lookup table that converts score dynamics, loudness, and MIDI velocity into one another. Nominal mappings are convenient for notation software and rendering systems, but they remain conventions. They should not be mistaken for measurement standards. This point is central to the whole dissertation because each chapter targets a different layer of the same broader expressive problem. Table~\ref{tab:bg_dynamics_compare} summarises the three dynamics representations that recur throughout this thesis, together with their temporal anchors, strengths, and limitations.

title: 把 onset 说法限定为本文的 Note On velocity

originals.query: MIDI velocity is a different kind of representation.
originals.text: MIDI velocity is a different kind of representation. It is attached to a note onset rather than to a phrase or region. In conventional MIDI performance data, a sounding note onset carries a discrete velocity value on a finite integer scale. In a chord, each note may have a different velocity. In a rapid passage, every note can carry its own local attack value. MIDI velocity is therefore a micro-level representation: it serialises note-level actions rather than summarising the expressive state of a passage.

variants.A: In this thesis, MIDI velocity means the Note On velocity associated with a note attack. MIDI also supports Note Off velocity and separate control messages, which are not the targets studied here. Each sounding note can therefore receive its own onset-velocity value, including notes played simultaneously in a chord.
variants.B: The target studied here is MIDI Note On velocity: a discrete control value attached to the start of a note. This definition is narrower than the full MIDI protocol, which also includes Note Off velocity, aftertouch, and continuous controllers. The thesis estimates one onset value per note rather than a time-varying control trajectory.
variants.C: The note-level target in this thesis is Note On velocity. It records or controls the attack of an individual note, so simultaneous notes may have different values. Other MIDI messages can describe release behaviour or changes during a note, but these remain outside the present target. This is why the velocity chapters preserve note events and estimate only an onset attribute.

title: humanisation 用一行定义

originals.query: Expressive performance rendering aims to generate expressive control signals
originals.text: Expressive performance rendering aims to generate expressive control signals from symbolic input. Many systems predict timing, dynamics, and sometimes articulation jointly \cite{jeong2019virtuosonet,borovik2023scoreperformer}. These models are important because they show that expressive performance can be learned from symbolic structure. At the same time, they reveal a practical limitation for the present thesis. Joint expressive rendering may alter more than the user wants. In production or corpus-upgrading settings, the desired operation is often narrower: preserve the notes and timing, and recover only the missing dynamics layer. This narrower, controllable objective is the entry point for Chapter~\ref{ch:velcomp}.

title: crescendo 已有定义，只补定位与范围

originals.query: They include static markings such as
originals.text: Dynamic markings are the conventional score vocabulary for notated loudness and dynamic change. They include static markings such as \textit{pp}, \textit{p}, \textit{mp}, \textit{mf}, \textit{f}, and \textit{ff}, as well as directional indications such as \textit{crescendo}, \textit{diminuendo}, and hairpins. Although a marking is printed at a specific visual position, its musical scope is usually broader than that position. A single \textit{p} may govern a phrase, a texture, or a formal region until a later marking or musical event changes the dynamic state. A crescendo indicates a tendency over a span, not an isolated value at one note.

originals.query: Computational modelling of dynamics has a long history
originals.text: Computational modelling of dynamics has a long history in expressive performance research \cite{cancinoChacon2018computational}. Rather than focusing only on note-level control, this line of work studies how performed loudness relates to symbolic dynamic markings and phrase structure. Kosta and collaborators showed both the usefulness and the ambiguity of this relationship \cite{kosta2014dynpiano,kosta2016mapping,kosta2018mazurkabl}. Other work has further analysed dynamic principles in piano performance \cite{jones2023probingdyn}.

F1 score is common because the class distribution is imbalanced and because some symbols occur much less frequently than others \cite{kosta2017thesis}. In the present thesis, beat-synchronous evaluation is especially important because it avoids arbitrary frame-level tolerance choices and aligns the prediction target with how the annotations are actually used in music notation.

originals.query: Velocity should be evaluated at note level
originals.text: Velocity should be evaluated at note level rather than by naive frame-wise error. Otherwise, long sustained notes dominate the metric. Standard statistics include mean absolute error and related dispersion measures \cite{kuo2021velocity,kim2024method}. However, numerical accuracy alone is not sufficient. A model can achieve a decent average error while producing over-smoothed or mechanically centred dynamics. Distribution-sensitive measures, visual inspection, and listening tests therefore play an important complementary role. This is especially evident in Chapter~\ref{ch:velcomp}, where perceptual differences are not always fully captured by raw error.

The segment duration is a key design variable in this formulation.
Because a MIDI performance often exceeds three minutes, we split each piece into shorter segments to keep the computation tractable.
The number of time frames \(T\) determines the temporal granularity of the matrix representation, so the timestep resolution is
\begin{equation}
\text{Resolution} = \frac{\text{Segment Duration}}{T}.
\label{eq:velcomp_resolution}
\end{equation}

title: 完整 AMT 集成作为未来方向，不虚报已验证性能

originals.query: This joint design serves two practical modes of use.
originals.text: Given a piano performance audio signal, the system predicts four synchronised output sequences on a frame grid: dynamic levels, dynamic change points, beats, and downbeats. The dynamic targets are the score-facing outputs, while beats and downbeats provide the metrical structure required to align these labels to a symbolic score. This joint design serves two practical modes of use. In the first mode, a reliable beat grid is already available from an aligned score or a score-level AMT system, and the predicted dynamic labels are attached to that grid. In the second mode, no score is available, and the model first predicts beats and downbeats by itself, then uses the estimated grid to place the dynamic labels.

originals.query: The broader direction is an AMT paradigm
originals.text: The broader direction is an AMT paradigm in which note detection is only the first layer. A musically useful transcription should not stop at pitch and onset. Dynamics is the layer studied in this thesis, but the same logic can extend to articulation, pedal, phrasing, and timbre.

originals.query: The change-point target is binary
originals.text: More specifically, the dynamic-level target is formulated as a six-class frame-wise prediction problem, including one \textit{blank} class before the first annotated marking and the five score-dynamics classes used in MazurkaBL: \textit{pp}, \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, \textit{f}, and \textit{ff}. The change-point target is binary and indicates whether a contextual transition between adjacent dynamic regimes occurs at a given time. Beats and downbeats are also binary frame-wise targets. At inference time, the frame-wise outputs are converted into beat-synchronous score annotations by sampling the dynamic class at beat locations and snapping detected change points to the nearest beat.

originals.query: Change points are determined in two stages.
originals.text: Change points are determined in two stages. First, we identify all frames whose change-point probability exceeds 75\%. Second, we snap each candidate to the nearest detected beat. This beat-snapping step is motivated by the annotation style of MazurkaBL, where dynamic markings are beat-aligned rather than freely placed in continuous time \cite{kosta2018mazurkabl}. The step also keeps evaluation consistent with prior work \cite{kosta2017thesis}.

A separate boundary head gives transitions their own supervision rather than deriving every change from fluctuations in the level sequence. The present experiments do not establish that it is the only valid formulation.
variants.C: A score-facing annotation needs both a level and a decision about when to write a new marking. originals.query: For beat and downbeat detection, we use
originals.text: The model outputs frame-wise probabilities, which are converted into discrete musical events through tailored post-processing. For beat and downbeat detection, we use the thresholding and local-maximum peak-picking steps of \cite{foscarin2024beat}: probabilities are thresholded at 50\%, and peak picking is applied within a 7-frame local neighbourhood (radius 3 at 50~fps). For dynamic markings, the dynamic level at each beat is determined by taking the \texttt{argmax} of the class probabilities at that frame. When an external beat grid is available, this sampling step is performed on that grid; otherwise, the model's own beat predictions are used, which gives the fully end-to-end mode considered in this chapter.

title: cross-dataset 是测迁移边界，不是分离风格因果

originals.query: The 5-fold MazurkaBL evaluation already gives a partial test
originals.text: The 5-fold MazurkaBL evaluation already gives a partial test of generalisation, because the folds are piece-disjoint and the model is always evaluated on unseen mazurkas within the same corpus. However, it remains an in-domain setting: performer pool, recording conditions, repertoire family, and annotation conventions are all inherited from MazurkaBL. We therefore add a stricter cross-dataset experiment on Vienna4x22 and Batik-plays-Mozart, using them as test-only corpora after the MazurkaBL training stage.

originals.query: Vienna4x22 shows that the symbolic prior itself matters
originals.text: The cross-dataset results make this distinction more concrete. If score dynamics were merely a continuous loudness variable relabelled into five fixed bins, an out-of-domain corpus with compatible audio quality would mainly cause smooth calibration errors. Instead, Vienna4x22 shows that the symbolic prior itself matters: a passage that is moderate in acoustic intensity may be notated as \textit{p}, \textit{mf}, or \textit{f} depending on the local phrase, edition, and corpus convention. A model trained on MazurkaBL carries a learned expectation about how often each of these labels should occur, and this expectation can become wrong even when the metrical grid remains reasonably stable. The model is therefore learning an acoustic, metrical, and editorial mapping at the same time.

A model trained on one corpus may learn its repertoire and annotation conventions as well as acoustic cues. Vienna4x22 and Batik-plays-Mozart test this combined shift, but their size and composition do not permit a balanced attribution to composer, performer, or recording conditions. The results are transfer diagnostics, not evidence of uniform generalisation.
variants.C: The external tests probe where the learned mapping stops transferring. They complement piece-disjoint MazurkaBL folds by changing several corpus conditions at once, including repertoire and score-label conventions. Their mixed outcomes therefore help delimit the claim: a perceptually motivated front-end does not remove stylistic or editorial dependence. A balanced study would be needed to separate those effects, but is outside the current experiment.

originals.query: This chapter takes a different and simpler route.
originals.text: This chapter takes a different and simpler route. Instead of training on synthesised audio with synthetic labels, the front-end estimator is trained directly against real performance audio. The synthesiser is involved at training time only as a differentiable interface that connects predicted velocities to a measurable property of the real recording. This avoids the synthesis-to-performance domain gap that dominates synthetic-data transfer pipelines, at the cost of needing a differentiable supervision interface that is reliable across the instruments of interest.

Expressive AMT extends beyond note transcription to capture the full aspects of a human performance. A comprehensive expressive transcription can be conceptually divided into three layers \cite{cancinoChacon2018computational}:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Timing Layer:} Captures the temporal elasticity of a performance, including macro-level tempo variation, beat-level timing, inter-onset intervals (IOIs), and micro-level articulation.
\item \textbf{Dynamic Layer:} Represents the intensity and energy of the music performance, bridging physical machine measurements (e.g., MIDI velocity) with semantic cognitive notations (e.g., score dynamic markings).
\item \textbf{Control Layer:} Includes instrument-specific techniques and acoustic modifiers, such as sustain pedalling, vibrato, reverberation, and amplifier configurations.
\end{itemize}
While all three layers are essential for the computational understanding of expressiveness in performance, this thesis singles out the \textbf{Dynamic Layer} as its primary focus. originals.text: The component ablations show that all major parts of the model contribute to the final performance, but not in the same way. The most diagnostic result is the removal of temporal scaling. Setting $s=1$ reduces the average F1 from 55.0 to 46.5, with particularly large drops in change-point F1 and downbeat F1. This indicates that the performance gain does not merely come from using a deeper convolutional encoder, but from exposing the downstream tasks to genuinely different temporal resolutions. Removing MMoE also degrades all four tasks, supporting the view that the four heads have different preference on the same shared latent. The overlap-based data augmentation gives a further improvement, which is expected for this dataset because change points and downbeats are sparse events. Overlapping audio segments increase the chance that such events appear in varied local contexts during training.

originals.query: not optimal for our tasks combination
originals.text: The temporal-scaling results give a detailed view of the multi-scale encoder. The reference architecture of \cite{li2023frame} uses a scaling factor of 3, but this value is not optimal for our tasks combination. With $s=3$, beat F1 and change-point F1 remain strong, but the average score is lower than the full model. Increasing the factor to $s=5$ gives the best overall balance. A slightly larger value, $s=7$, remains competitive and gives the second-best average score, but further increasing the factor to $s=9$ causes a clear degradation, especially for downbeats. This pattern suggests that the model needs a sufficiently coarse branch to capture long-range dynamic context, but excessive temporal compression begins to remove information that cannot be fully recovered for event localisation. The best value is therefore not simply the largest receptive field, but the best compromise between contextual abstraction and temporal precision.
